The comparison of treatment success versus treatment failure, relapse, or death, as well as the comparison of success versus treatment failure, relapse, death, or loss to follow-up, and death versus treatment failure, relapse, or success, highlights the need for precise definitions and outcomes in evaluating surgical interventions for multidrug-resistant tuberculosis (MDR-TB) and extensively drug-resistant tuberculosis (XDR-TB). 2. The types of surgeries considered include lobectomy, segmentectomy, and wedge resection. It is critical to define non-response and adverse outcomes of surgery, as well as the extent of disease and the expertise of the centers or practitioners performing the surgeries, to ensure external validity. 3. The conditions under which resection surgery is indicated or contraindicated, and whether it is performed before or after culture conversion, are essential considerations in the decision-making process. 4. The role of surgery in MDR-TB and XDR-TB treatment must be better defined, including when to operate, the type of intervention, and its impact on treatment outcomes. 5. A meta-analysis of surgical interventions demonstrated a statistically significant improvement in cure and successful treatment outcomes among patients who underwent surgery. However, individual patient data analysis revealed that partial lung resection was associated with significantly higher treatment success rates compared to no surgery, while pneumonectomy did not show better outcomes than non-surgical treatment. 6. Selection bias is a potential limitation, as only patients deemed healthy enough for surgery were included. Additionally, people living with HIV were excluded from the individual patient data analysis. 7. Patients with XDR-TB who underwent surgery had significantly worse outcomes, likely due to confounding factors. Mortality rates did not differ significantly between surgical and non-surgical groups. 8. There was insufficient data on adverse events or surgical complications to perform a comprehensive analysis. 9. The WHO Guideline Development Group suggests that elective partial lung resection (lobectomy or wedge resection) may be used alongside an approved MDR-TB regimen, but this recommendation is conditional and based on very low certainty of evidence. 10. Partial lung resection is recommended only in settings with good surgical facilities, trained and experienced surgeons, and careful selection of appropriate surgical candidates. 11. Monitoring and evaluation should include definitions of extensive disease, parameters for assessing response, non-response, adverse outcomes, and sequelae of surgery, as well as the optimal timing for surgery after culture conversion. 12. Research priorities include identifying conditions that indicate or contraindicate resection surgery, selecting appropriate patients, and determining the type of disease suitable for surgical intervention. 13. Short MDR-TB regimens based on the Bangladesh regimen have shown promising results in patients with no prior exposure to second-line drugs and baseline susceptibility to fluoroquinolones and pyrazinamide. However, data on relapse is limited, though available evidence suggests relapse is rare. 14. Standardized short MDR-TB regimens demonstrated higher treatment success rates compared to longer regimens, particularly when death and loss to follow-up were included as unsuccessful outcomes. 15. Individual patient data meta-analyses showed consistently better outcomes with short MDR-TB regimens, though confidence limits overlapped. Patients with fluoroquinoloneor pyrazinamide-resistant MDR-TB had worse outcomes in both short and long regimen groups. 16. The intensive phase of short MDR-TB regimens typically lasted at least four months, with continuation phases lasting five to eight months. Regimens included kanamycin, moxifloxacin or gatifloxacin, high-dose isoniazid, prothionamide, clofazimine, pyrazinamide, and ethambutol. 17. All treatment was directly observed, and many patients were hospitalized for part of the treatment. Outcomes such as cure, treatment completion, failure, death, and default were reported in all studies. 18. Relapse, defined as a positive culture post-treatment, was rare and counted as treatment failure in analyses. Short MDR-TB regimens showed higher success rates compared to longer regimens, even when stratified by baseline drug susceptibility. 19. The WHO recommends short MDR-TB regimens for patients with baseline susceptibility to fluoroquinolones and pyrazinamide, provided they have not been previously treated with second-line drugs. However, data on relapse and long-term outcomes remain limited.
